gloss_terse: sin-offering (Aramaic cognate of Hebrew חַטָּאת)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic term appears in Ezra 6:17 where the returned exiles offer sacrifices at the dedication of the rebuilt temple. The word is the Aramaic equivalent of the common Hebrew חַטָּאת (sin-offering), reflecting the bilingual nature of Ezra-Nehemiah. The Ketiv reads חַטָּיָא while the Qere offers חַטָּאָה, both functioning as loan-words from the sacrificial vocabulary that transcends linguistic boundaries in Second Temple worship contexts.

gloss_terse: heat, rage, wrath; also venom, poison (from root meaning 'to be hot')
gloss_readable: This powerful term captures the physical sensation of burning heat and its psychological parallel in human rage. The semantic range extends from literal fever (as in Hosea 7:5, 'wine-fever') to the metaphorical heat of divine wrath that appears repeatedly in prophetic judgment oracles. Interestingly, cognate languages preserve both the 'heat' and 'poison' senses—Arabic and Syriac can mean venom, while Akkadian imtu denotes breath or poison. The term frequently appears with possessive suffixes in contexts of God's anger being poured out, creating vivid imagery of wrath as something hot, consuming, and life-threatening.

gloss_terse: personal name meaning 'son of mercy' — an officer of Solomon
gloss_readable: This theophoric personal name appears in 1 Kings 4:10 as one of Solomon's twelve district officers responsible for provisioning the royal household. The name literally means 'son of mercy' or 'son of chesed,' embodying the Hebrew concept of covenant loyalty and kindness. Such names in ancient Israel often reflected parental piety or aspirations for the child's character, and the chesed element connects to one of the most theologically rich words in Hebrew Scripture.

gloss_terse: (stone) heap (Aramaic term used in Genesis 31:47 parallel to Hebrew גַּל־עֵד)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic word appears in the famous boundary-setting scene between Jacob and Laban in Genesis 31:47. Laban speaks Aramaic, calling the witness-heap 'Yegar-Sahadutha,' while Jacob uses the Hebrew equivalent 'Galeed.' Both terms mean 'heap of witness,' marking a covenant boundary. The bilingual wordplay in this passage reflects the linguistic and ethnic divide between the Aramaic-speaking peoples of Mesopotamia and the Hebrew-speaking descendants of Abraham, even as they make peace through shared covenant practices.

gloss_terse: testimony, witness (Aramaic cognate, appears in Genesis 31:47 parallel to Hebrew עֵד)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic term for 'testimony' or 'witness' appears in the emphatic state as part of Laban's compound name for the covenant heap in Genesis 31:47. The root is cognate with Hebrew שָׂהֵד and related to widespread Semitic vocabulary for witnessing and testimony (Syriac, Arabic shahida). The word appears in the famous bilingual pun where the stone-heap serves as a 'witness' between Jacob and Laban, commemorating their covenant. Egyptian Aramaic documents frequently use related forms for witnesses in legal contexts.

gloss_terse: see, perceive, look at; appear, be seen; provide, consider (primary verb of visual perception)
gloss_readable: This is the foundational Hebrew verb for seeing, appearing over 1,300 times throughout Scripture. Beyond physical sight, it encompasses mental perception, divine revelation, and providential care. The verb appears in pivotal moments: God 'seeing' human affliction (Genesis 16, 29), Abraham naming the place 'the LORD will see/provide' (Genesis 22:14), and prophets being called 'seers.' Cognate across all Semitic languages, it can mean passive appearance ('be seen') as well as active observation. The breadth from literal eyesight to spiritual insight makes this one of Scripture's most theologically loaded verbs.

gloss_terse: rightness, righteousness, justice; what is right, just, or normal in conduct and character
gloss_readable: This noun denotes what is straight, right, and just—both in the concrete sense of honest weights and measures and in the moral-theological sense of righteous character and just governance. It describes right paths (Psalm 23:3), just legal judgments, and ultimately God's own righteousness that becomes the standard for covenant faithfulness. The term appears in legal contexts (just weights, Leviticus 19:36), royal contexts (kings judging in righteousness), and cultic contexts (right sacrifices). Frequently paralleled with מִשְׁפָּט (justice) and צְדָקָה (righteousness), it anchors Israel's ethical vocabulary in the metaphor of straightness versus crookedness.

gloss_terse: completeness, soundness, welfare, peace; well-being in all dimensions of life
gloss_readable: This rich term encompasses wholeness, health, prosperity, peace, and relational harmony—far more than mere absence of conflict. It appears in greetings ('Is it peace/well with you?'), describes physical safety and bodily health, and carries theological weight as God's gift of comprehensive flourishing. The semantic range includes completeness in number, soundness of body, material welfare, and especially peaceful relationships. When Moses promises peace-offerings or Israelites inquire after one another's שָׁלוֹם, they invoke a vision of integrated well-being that touches every dimension of human existence under God's blessing.

gloss_terse: there, thither; in that place or to that place (locative/directional adverb)
gloss_readable: This common Hebrew adverb marks spatial location ('there') or direction ('to there'). It appears in countless narrative and poetic contexts, often positioned early in the sentence for emphasis. The word can be used literally (Genesis 2:8, God placed man 'there' in the garden) or in more abstract senses ('there' in Sheol, Psalm 139:8). Hebrew poetry exploits the word's rhythmic potential through repetition ('and there... and there') to build literary effect. Though simple in meaning, its frequency and versatility make it a key building block of Hebrew narrative style.

gloss_terse: dove, pigeon (the bird; often used in sacrificial contexts or similes)
gloss_readable: The dove appears both as Noah's messenger after the flood (Genesis 8) and as a standard sacrificial bird throughout Levitical law, where 'young pigeons' (בְּנֵי יוֹנָה) are prescribed for purification offerings. Beyond cultic usage, doves serve as similes: Ephraim is 'like a silly dove' easily snared (Hosea 7:11), returning exiles come like doves to their windows (Isaiah 60:8), and the beloved in Song of Songs is addressed as 'my dove.' The bird's associations include innocence, simplicity, vulnerability, and swift return—themes that resonate through both prophetic and wisdom literature.

gloss_terse: remain behind, delay, tarry, linger (often with negative implication of unwelcome delay)
gloss_readable: This verb describes staying behind or delaying when forward movement is expected. Genesis 32:5 uses it for Jacob's tarrying with Laban; Genesis 24:56 has Abraham's servant refusing to delay his return journey. The Piel intensifies the sense: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming?' (Judges 5:28). Isaiah 46:13 and Daniel 9:19 assure that God's salvation will not tarry, contrasting divine reliability with human procrastination. The word often carries urgency: someone is late, something is overdue, the expected has not yet arrived—and patience is wearing thin.

gloss_terse: textual error in 1 Samuel 4:13 (Ketiv) for יָד 'hand' (Qere)
gloss_readable: This entry represents a scribal variant or textual corruption in 1 Samuel 4:13. The Ketiv (written text) reads יך but the Qere (read aloud) corrects to יָד ('hand'). Such Ketiv-Qere notations preserve both the received consonantal text and the traditional reading, allowing scholars to track scribal variations. In this case, the correction is straightforward: a letter was likely miscopied, and the Qere restores the intended word 'hand.'

gloss_terse: touch (dubious lemma; Judges 16:26 Ketiv, likely textual error for מָשַׁשׁ)
gloss_readable: This verb appears only in Judges 16:26 where Samson asks to 'feel' the pillars he will pull down. However, most scholars regard it as a textual error rather than a genuine word. The Ketiv reads וְהֵימִשֵׁנִי while the Qere offers וַהֲמִישֵׁנִי. BDB suggests the intended root is מָשַׁשׁ ('to feel, grope'), a much more common verb appropriate to Samson's blindness. This represents the kind of marginal lexical entry that exists only to document and explain a problematic manuscript reading.

gloss_terse: wood, forest, thicket; wooded area or densely treed land
gloss_readable: This noun denotes a wood, forest, or thicket—places dense with trees that can be felled for timber or serve as domains of danger and mystery. Joshua 17 describes the hill country as 'forest' to be cleared; 2 Samuel 18 sets Absalom's defeat in 'the forest of Ephraim.' Forests in ancient Israel were both resource (timber for building) and threat (wild beasts, ambush sites). Jeremiah 10:3 speaks of cutting 'wood from the forest' for idol-carving. The term appears in geographical names and carries associations with wilderness, danger, and the boundary between civilization and untamed nature.

gloss_terse: cowed, subdued (adjective; Psalm 10:10 Qere)
gloss_readable: This rare adjective appears in Psalm 10:10 (Qere) describing the 'cowed ones'—people beaten down and subdued by the wicked. The Ketiv offers a different reading (חלכאים), but the Qere suggests חֵל בָּאִים, 'a host of cowed ones,' painting a picture of the vulnerable and oppressed who fall into the hands of violent oppressors. The textual uncertainty reflects the psalm's difficult transmission, though the theme of the wicked preying on the helpless remains clear in context.

gloss_terse: support, root, stock (of a tree; Psalm 80:16, textually uncertain)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun appears only in Psalm 80:16, likely meaning the 'root' or 'stock' of a vine—the support structure from which growth springs. The psalm depicts Israel as a vine God planted, now ravaged by enemies, and the plea is for God to protect what 'your right hand has planted.' However, textual uncertainties abound: some suggest reading it as a verb ('establish it'), others point to Syriac cognates for 'support.' The ambiguity reflects the challenges of reconstructing rare botanical terminology from ancient poetry, though the image of rootedness and support remains consistent with the psalm's vineyard metaphor.

gloss_terse: personal name—father of Paltiel, Michal's second husband (1 Samuel 25:44; 2 Samuel 3:15)
gloss_readable: Laish appears as the father of Paltiel (or Palti), the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal after David fled. This sets up the later painful scene in 2 Samuel 3:15 where David demands Michal's return, and Paltiel follows weeping. The name appears with textual variants (Ketiv and Qere differ in 2 Samuel 3:15), and the Septuagint offers widely varying transliterations. The personal drama of Michal's forced remarriage and retrieval gains pathos when we see Paltiel's father's name attached to this minor character who loved a woman he had to surrender.

gloss_terse: discern, perceive, understand; have insight or comprehension (with senses or mind)
gloss_readable: This verb encompasses perception through the senses and understanding through the mind, moving fluidly between seeing clearly, hearing attentively, and grasping intellectually. It can denote literal sensory perception (eyes that discern, Psalm 19:12 asking 'who can discern his errors?') or deeper cognitive insight (Daniel 10:1 'understanding the vision'). The root appears across Semitic languages with connotations of separation and distinctness—to discern is to distinguish, to perceive differences. Wisdom literature prizes this capacity: 'the wise will understand' (Daniel 12:10). The verb's theological weight lies in its connection to wisdom, revelation, and the gift of spiritual insight.

gloss_terse: tower (variant form; 2 Samuel 22:51 Qere for Ketiv מַגְדִּיל)
gloss_readable: This noun form appears in 2 Samuel 22:51 (Qere) meaning 'tower,' where God is praised as 'a tower of salvation for his king.' The Ketiv reads מַגְדִּיל ('magnifies'), and the parallel text in Psalm 18:51 has מַגְדִּל. The image of God as a defensive tower or fortress is common in David's psalms, evoking military security and refuge. The Qere preserves an alternate reading that may reflect different manuscript traditions or interpretative options for this victory hymn, where God's protective strength is celebrated after deliverance from enemies.

gloss_terse: measure, apportionment; also cloth, garment (as extended or wide)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes 'measure' in the sense of an assigned portion or allotment (Jeremiah 13:25, 'the portion of your measures'), but also extends to mean a cloth or garment—something spread out or extended. Judges 5:10 may refer to carpets or cloths for sitting, while 1 Samuel 4:12 describes torn garments as a sign of mourning. The semantic link between 'measure' and 'cloth' lies in the idea of extension and dimension. The word's flexibility reflects the concrete, material world of ancient Israel where measurements and textiles both shaped daily life.

gloss_terse: sufficiency, enough; what is adequate or sufficient for a need
gloss_readable: This noun expresses 'enough' or 'sufficiency'—the state of having what is needed. Malachi 3:10 promises blessings 'until there is not sufficiency,' meaning inexhaustible abundance. Esther 1:18 warns of 'plenty of contempt and wrath' as a consequence of the queen's defiance. The term often appears in the construct state with a genitive, indicating sufficiency 'for' something or someone (Exodus 36:5, 'more than enough for the work'). The word's rarity and contextual usage suggest a technical or formal register, marking careful measurement of adequacy rather than casual abundance.

gloss_terse: foundation, appointment; something established or set in place (Isaiah 30:32, Ezekiel 41:8)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes 'foundation' in both physical and metaphorical senses. Isaiah 30:32 speaks of 'the appointed rod' (rod of foundation/appointment), suggesting divine decree or ordained punishment. Ezekiel 41:8 (Qere) uses the plural to describe 'foundations' of the temple structure, though textual difficulties abound. The Ketiv may intend a Pual participle meaning 'furnished with foundations.' The ambiguity reflects the word's rarity, but the core sense of something established, founded, or appointed by divine decree remains consistent with the root יָסַד ('to found, establish').

gloss_terse: row, rank, battle-line; arrangement in order (especially military formation)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes an ordered arrangement, especially a battle-line or military formation. First Samuel 17 uses it repeatedly for the 'ranks' of Israel's army that Goliath defies—'the ranks of the living God' (v. 26). It can also mean a row or arrangement of lamps (Exodus 39:37, 'lamps arranged in a row'). The term captures the idea of deliberate ordering: soldiers standing in formation, lamps set in sequence, organized arrays. The phrase 'battle-line against battle-line' (1 Samuel 17:21) evokes the formal, almost ritualized confrontation of ancient Near Eastern warfare.

gloss_terse: booty, plunder, spoil (what is seized in war or violence)
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes plunder or spoil taken by violence or conquest. Second Kings 21:14 warns that Judah will become 'booty and prey' to enemies; Zephaniah 1:13 describes possessions becoming 'plunder' in divine judgment. The term appears in prophetic oracles of reversal, where those who plundered will themselves be plundered (Jeremiah 30:16). Isaiah 42:22-24 uses the word to describe Israel's humiliation: they have become 'prey' and 'plunder' because of sin. The vocabulary of seizure and spoil pervades prophetic judgment literature, turning the logic of conquest inside out.

gloss_terse: fruit (especially 'fruit of lips'; Ketiv in Isaiah 57:19 for Qere נִיב)
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Isaiah 57:19 (Ketiv) meaning 'fruit,' specifically 'fruit of lips'—a metaphor for speech, praise, or thanksgiving. The Qere reads נִיב, but both forms convey the same sense: words as produce of the mouth. Hebrews 13:15 later picks up this imagery: 'the fruit of lips that confess his name.' The agricultural metaphor for human speech—lips as trees bearing fruit—pervades biblical poetry, linking verbal expression to the generative, life-giving processes of creation.

gloss_terse: preserved, guarded (adjective; Isaiah 49:6 Ketiv, Qere reads נְצוּרֵי)
gloss_readable: This adjective form appears only in Isaiah 49:6 (Ketiv) as part of the phrase describing the Servant's mission: to 'raise up the preserved of Israel.' The Qere reads נְצוּרֵי (from נָצַר, 'to watch, guard, preserve'), referring to the surviving remnant—those whom God has kept safe through judgment and exile. The Servant's task extends beyond Israel to be 'a light to the nations,' but begins with restoring the 'preserved ones,' the faithful remnant. This theme of the guarded remnant runs through Isaiah's theology of judgment and restoration.

gloss_terse: textual variant in Hosea 10:10 (Ketiv/Qere uncertain; likely עֲוֹנֹתָם 'their iniquities')
gloss_readable: This entry documents a textual puzzle in Hosea 10:10. The Qere reads עוֹנֹתָם (possibly plural of עוֹנָה, though unclear), while the Ketiv offers עֵינֹתָם. Scholars generally emend to עֲוֹנֹתָם ('their iniquities'), which fits the context of divine judgment and chastisement. The passage warns that nations will gather against Israel 'when I discipline them for their double iniquity.' The textual uncertainty reflects the challenges of preserving and interpreting difficult prophetic oracles, but the theme of punishment for sin remains unmistakable.

gloss_terse: spring, fountain (of water); natural water source
gloss_readable: This common noun denotes a spring or fountain—a natural source of fresh water, vital in the semi-arid landscapes of ancient Israel. Genesis 24 features the spring where Abraham's servant meets Rebekah; Genesis 16:7 places Hagar at 'a spring of water in the wilderness.' Deuteronomy 8:7 describes the promised land as blessed with 'springs and fountains.' Springs were places of encounter, life, and provision, often named and remembered in Israel's geography and story. Proverbs 8:28 even speaks of 'the fountains of the deep' as part of creation's structure, linking springs to the cosmic order God established.

gloss_terse: City of Palms (epithet for Jericho; associated with date palms)
gloss_readable: This descriptive phrase serves as an alternate name for Jericho, highlighting the city's lush vegetation and date palm groves in an otherwise arid region. Deuteronomy 34:3 uses the epithet in describing the view from Mount Nebo: 'the plain of the Valley of Jericho, the city of palms.' Judges 1:16 and 3:13 also use the term. Jericho's abundant water supply (from nearby springs) made it an oasis, and the date palms became iconic. The name evokes fertility, blessing, and the contrast between Israel's desert wanderings and the fruitful land they were entering.

gloss_terse: ascent, stairway (Ezekiel 40:26 Ketiv; Qere reads עֹלוֹתָיו; likely error for מַעֲלָתוֹ)
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Ezekiel 40:26 (Ketiv) as part of the temple vision, apparently meaning 'ascent' or 'stairway'—the steps leading up to a gate. However, the Ketiv is singular while the Qere offers a plural, and many scholars emend to מַעֲלָתוֹ ('its steps'), the more common term for stairway in Ezekiel's architectural descriptions. The textual confusion reflects the complexity of Ezekiel's visionary temple blueprint, where precise architectural vocabulary is sometimes uncertain. The core image remains: a stepped ascent into the sacred space.

gloss_terse: people, nation; a body of persons united by kinship, geography, or covenant
gloss_readable: This foundational noun denotes 'people' in the sense of a cohesive group—whether ethnic nation, tribal confederation, or covenant community. It can refer specifically to Israel as 'God's people' (Exodus 3:7, 'I have seen the affliction of my people') or generically to any nation or ethnic group. The plural עַמִּים means 'peoples' or 'nations' in the international sense. The root likely connects to ideas of kinship, unity, and social bonding. Theologically, the term carries immense weight: Israel is called 'my people,' marking covenant relationship, while the nations are summoned to recognize Yahweh's sovereignty over all peoples.

gloss_terse: neck; used in epithet 'sons of Anak'—long-necked (tall) men, a race of giants
gloss_readable: This noun means 'neck' but appears primarily in the phrase 'sons of Anak' (בְּנֵי הָעֲנָק), describing a legendary race of tall, powerful people inhabiting Canaan before Israel's conquest. Numbers 13:33 reports the spies' fearful reaction: 'we saw the Nephilim (the sons of Anak come from the Nephilim), and we seemed like grasshoppers.' The epithet 'long-necked' suggests height and imposing stature. Joshua 15:14 and Judges 1:20 recount Caleb's defeat of three Anakites at Hebron. The Anakites became symbolic of formidable enemies that God nonetheless enabled Israel to overcome, demonstrating divine power over seemingly invincible foes.

gloss_terse: cryptic phrase in Jeremiah 51:1 (Leb-kamai = 'heart of my adversaries'; coded reference)
gloss_readable: This entry represents an Atbash cipher in Jeremiah 51:1 where לֵב קָמָי ('Leb-kamai,' meaning 'heart of those rising against me') stands as a cryptic designation for Babylon or the Chaldeans. Atbash substitutes letters in reverse alphabetical order, so כשדים (Kasdim, Chaldeans) becomes קמי. The prophet uses coded language, possibly for rhetorical effect or to avoid direct naming during dangerous political circumstances. Scholarly debate continues over whether this is intentional cipher or textual corruption, but the cryptic quality adds to the oracle's mystique as Jeremiah pronounces judgment on Israel's oppressor.

gloss_terse: assemble (as a קָהָל, congregation/assembly); gather together for religious, military, or civic purposes
gloss_readable: This denominative verb (from קָהָל 'assembly') means to gather as a formal assembly or congregation. It appears in the Niphal for communal gathering: for warfare (Joshua 22:12, Judges 20:1), for rebellion (Numbers 16:3, the Korah incident), or for worship (Joshua 18:1, assembling at Shiloh). The verb implies organized, purposeful gathering—not random crowds but structured assemblies with shared intent. Esther 8-9 uses it for the Jews gathering to defend themselves. The term captures Israel's communal identity: they are a people who assemble, who act collectively before God and in history.

gloss_terse: see, perceive, look at; appear, be seen; provide, consider (primary verb of visual perception)
gloss_readable: This is the foundational Hebrew verb for seeing, appearing over 1,300 times throughout Scripture. Beyond physical sight, it encompasses mental perception, divine revelation, and providential care. The verb appears in pivotal moments: God 'seeing' human affliction, Abraham naming the place 'the LORD will see/provide' (Genesis 22:14), and prophets being called 'seers.' Cognate across all Semitic languages, it can mean passive appearance ('be seen') as well as active observation. The breadth from literal eyesight to spiritual insight makes this one of Scripture's most theologically loaded verbs. The Hiphil causative means 'show' or 'let see,' and Niphal passive means 'appear' or 'be seen.'

gloss_terse: overcome (by wine or emotion; rare verb, possibly related to Arabic 'overcome')
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears only in Psalm 78:65 in a striking simile: 'Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a hero overcome by wine' (or 'shouting from wine,' depending on interpretation). The root may be related to Arabic رَانَ ('to overcome') or alternatively to רָנַן ('to shout'). The context depicts God rousing himself to fight for Israel after a period of apparent inactivity. Whether the image is of a warrior shaking off wine-induced sleep or a warrior shouting in battle-fury, the metaphor conveys sudden, overwhelming divine intervention. The textual and etymological uncertainties reflect the verse's bold anthropomorphism.

gloss_terse: chain (for captives; Ezekiel 7:23, textually uncertain; also 1 Kings 6:21 Qere)
gloss_readable: This noun appears in Ezekiel 7:23 in the command 'make the chain,' apparently referring to chains for captives as Babylon prepares to haul Judah into exile. However, the text is notoriously difficult, and scholars propose various emendations. First Kings 6:21 (Qere) also reads רַתּוּקוֹת זָהָב ('chains of gold') adorning the temple's inner sanctuary, though the Ketiv differs. The vocabulary of chains connects to themes of bondage, captivity, and decorative metalwork. The textual uncertainties surrounding this rare term illustrate the challenges of reconstructing ancient Hebrew technical vocabulary for metallurgy and bondage.

gloss_terse: level plain (geographical term; Genesis 14:5 in Shaveh-Kiriathaim)
gloss_readable: This noun meaning 'level plain' or 'valley' appears in Genesis 14:5 as part of the place name 'Shaveh-Kiriathaim,' where Chedorlaomer defeats the Emim during his military campaign. The term denotes flat, open land suitable for battle or settlement. Some read Kiriathaim as appositional ('the plain, namely Kiriathaim') while others take Shaveh as a common noun ('the plain of Kiriathaim'). The geographical reference locates ancient conflicts in Transjordan, though precise identification remains uncertain. The term evokes the strategic importance of level ground for military movements in ancient Near Eastern warfare.
